paras: The attempted lynching of George Mills took place at Hannibal, Missouri, in December 1881, when a posse of fifteen men who seized Mills on an accusation of attempted rape barely kept him from being lynched. Mills was handed over to the authorities, and the story ran as a short wire item in several out-of-state papers on December 21.

According to the wire report, Mills was accused of attempting to rape Mrs. A. Fink on the highway at Hannibal. The dispatch said he presented a revolver, which she grasped, and that in the scuffle it went off and took off part of one of her fingers. Her screams were said to have driven him off, and she told her husband when she got home.

Fifteen men then searched for Mills and found him at his father's house. By the posse's account as carried in the wire, Mills refused to come out and fired at them, after which they broke down the door and disarmed and overpowered him. "With difficulty the captors saved Mills from lynching," the Wheeling Register's version said, "but he was finally handed over to the authorities." The report does not say who wanted to lynch him or where in Hannibal this happened, and no injury to Mills is described.
No report of a charge, trial or later proceedings against Mills was found in the coverage.

Every surviving account is the same dispatch, datelined St. Louis, December 20, in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer, the Wheeling Register and the St. Paul Daily Globe, and Hannibal in the Memphis Daily Appeal. The Wheeling papers ran it inside Missouri crime roundups headed "Missouri Miseries" and "Crimes," while the Appeal and the Globe gave it its own heading, "Attempt at Rape" and "Attempted Rape." The text treated the accusation as fact, called Mills "the ruffian" and closed with the remark that "Mills is a hard case."

None of the versions names the race of Mills, Mrs. Fink or the posse. The Appeal's punctuation shifted the phrase "with difficulty" onto the overpowering of Mills, making the rescue from lynching read as routine, while the other versions put the difficulty in saving him.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of George Mills
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A posse of fifteen seized Mills at his father's house and he was saved 'with difficulty' from being lynched before being handed to the authorities (A1, A2).

No one was killed: the wire says the captors saved Mills from lynching and turned him over to the authorities (A1, A2); the threat came from a group of fifteen pursuing him on an accusation of attempted rape, so this is an attempted lynching, not a completed one.
All four papers print the same December 20 wire text (A1, A2, A3, A4); no independent or local account was found.

accounts.label: Wire report (St. Louis/Hannibal, Dec. 20)
accounts.gist: Mills attacked Mrs. Fink with a revolver on the highway; fifteen men found him at his father's house, broke in after he fired at them, and with difficulty kept him from being lynched before handing him to the authorities.

framing.detail: Printed as one item in Missouri crime roundups ('Missouri Miseries', 'Crimes'), treating the accusation as fact and closing 'Mills is a hard case'.
The Memphis Daily Appeal ran it alone under 'Attempt at Rape' with a Hannibal dateline.

conflicts.note: A punctuation variant of one wire text; two of three opened versions put the difficulty in the rescue from lynching.

record_check.dossier: No paper states Mills's race; leave unknown.
The papers name only Hannibal, Missouri; the county is not printed.
Dispatch dated December 20, 1881; the assault and capture were on or shortly before that date.
Search, exchange (Mills fired at the posse), door broken down, seizure, near-lynching; 'siege' overstates a single forced entry.
Mills was in the posse's hands (not officers') when the lynching was averted, then handed to the authorities.
Four white papers ran the wire on December 21 (Wheeling Intelligencer, Wheeling Register, Memphis Daily Appeal, St. Paul Daily Globe).
